paragraphs: Pride and Prejudice, published in 1813, is Jane Austen's most beloved novel and one of the most beloved novels ever written in English. It tells the story of Elizabeth Bennet, the sharpest and liveliest of five unmarried sisters, and Mr. Darcy, the proudest and richest young man in the county, and how these two brilliant, stubborn people misunderstand each other, wound each other, and finally learn to see clearly. It is a comedy of manners, a love story, and a quietly radical examination of how we judge other people.

Austen wrote it in her twenties, revised it for years, and published it anonymously, as a lady would in those days. The world she describes is small: a few country families, their drawing rooms, their balls, their endless conversations about marriage. But within that small world she created characters as vivid as any in literature, and dialogue so sparkling that readers have been quoting it for two hundred years. The novel's subject is announced in its title: the pride of Darcy, the prejudice of Elizabeth, and the education both must undergo.

What makes the book immortal is Elizabeth herself. She is witty, intelligent, and completely confident in her own judgment, and the novel's great drama is watching that confidence collapse as she discovers how wrong she has been. Every reader who has ever misjudged someone, nursed a prejudice, or been humbled by the truth will recognize themselves in her story. It begins with the most famous first sentence in English fiction, and it never puts a foot wrong from there to its perfect ending.

Jane Austen herself was the daughter of a country clergyman, one of eight children, and she lived the quiet life she describes: no marriage, no great adventures, only a sharp eye and a sharper pen. She wrote in the family's sitting room, hiding her manuscripts when visitors called, and she saw only four of her six novels published in her lifetime. She died at forty-one, largely unknown. Yet her style, ironic, precise, and devastatingly witty, has never been surpassed. She does not describe battles or shipwrecks. Her drama happens in drawing rooms, in a raised eyebrow, in a sentence that means the opposite of what it says. And somehow it contains the whole of human nature.
Reader, prepare to be delighted, provoked, and quietly transformed. You are about to meet the wittiest heroine in English fiction, the proudest hero, and the most satisfying love story ever told.
chapters.title: About This Book

paragraphs: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife." With that single glittering sentence, half serious and half mocking, Jane Austen opens her novel and sets its whole machinery in motion. The sentence pretends to be about the rich young man. It is really about everyone else: the mothers hunting husbands for their daughters, the neighbours watching every new arrival, the whole marriage market of rural England.

The family at the center of it is the Bennets of Longbourn: Mr. Bennet, clever, lazy, and sarcastic, who has long since given up managing his household; Mrs. Bennet, foolish, nervous, and loud, whose entire existence is devoted to marrying off her five daughters; and the daughters themselves. Jane, the eldest, is beautiful and sweet, too good to suspect evil in anyone. Elizabeth, the second, is the heroine: quick, observant, and dangerously sure of her own cleverness. Then Mary, Kitty, and Lydia, younger, sillier, and, in Lydia's case, headed for real trouble.

The shadow over the Bennet household has a name: Mr. Collins. He is the distant cousin who will inherit Longbourn when Mr. Bennet dies, a pompous young clergyman with a patroness, the terrifying Lady Catherine de Bourgh, whose name he drops into every second sentence. Mr. Collins arrives with a proposal of his own: he intends to marry one of the Bennet daughters, as a kind of compensation for inheriting their home. He first fixes on Jane, then, told she is taken, turns to Elizabeth, and proposes with a speech so absurd, so stuffed with self-importance, that Elizabeth can barely keep a straight face as she refuses him.

Mr. Bennet, hearing of the refusal, supports his favourite daughter with rare decisiveness. His wife, predictably, is hysterical. But Elizabeth has escaped one folly only to watch her friend Charlotte Lucas accept Mr. Collins instead, marrying for security and a home of her own. Elizabeth is shocked, then thoughtful. Charlotte's choice is not romantic, but it is rational, and it forces Elizabeth to confront an uncomfortable truth: in a world where women cannot earn their own fortunes, marriage is not only about love. It is about survival. This is the steel beneath Austen's comedy, and it never leaves the novel.

The Bennets have a problem that shapes everything: their house and estate are entailed away from the female line, which means that when Mr. Bennet dies, everything goes to a distant cousin, the absurd Mr. Collins. The daughters must marry, and marry well, or face poverty. Into this anxious household comes the news that Netherfield Park, a fine estate nearby, has been rented by a young man of large fortune from the north of England: Mr. Bingley.

Mr. Bingley is everything a mother could wish: rich, handsome, cheerful, and amiable. He brings with him his sisters and his closest friend, Mr. Darcy, who is richer still, handsomer in a severe way, and so proud and silent that the whole neighbourhood decides within an evening that he is the most disagreeable man in the world. Mrs. Bennet immediately sets her sights on Bingley for Jane. Elizabeth watches them all with amusement, little suspecting that the disagreeable Mr. Darcy is about to become the most important person in her life.

The Bennets' marriage is itself a warning about what Elizabeth is fighting. Mr. Bennet married a pretty, foolish girl and has spent twenty years regretting it, amusing himself with sarcasm while his household runs wild. Mrs. Bennet, for her part, lives in a permanent flutter of nerves and schemes, convinced that the world is conspiring to leave her daughters spinsters. Between them they have produced five girls with almost no guidance and no fortune. Elizabeth, the cleverest of them, has learned to laugh at her parents, but the laughter has a sharp edge. She is determined not to repeat their mistake, not to marry without love, and not to marry without respect. It is a noble resolve, and it will be tested to the limit.
chapters.title: A Truth Universally Acknowledged

paragraphs: The assembly ball at Meryton is the novel's first great set piece, and the night Elizabeth Bennet's prejudice is born. The whole neighbourhood is there, the Bennets are there in force, and all eyes are on the Netherfield party. Bingley dances every dance, charms every lady, and falls visibly in love with Jane, the most beautiful girl in the room. His friend Darcy stands apart, tall and grave, dancing only a few times and speaking to almost no one.

Elizabeth, lively and pretty, catches Darcy's eye for a moment, and she overhears what he says to Bingley when Bingley urges him to dance with her. "She a beauty! I should as soon call her mother a wit." The words are careless, arrogant, and unforgivable, and Elizabeth never forgets them. She tells the story afterward with laughter, making a joke of it, but the wound goes deep. From that night, she has Darcy fixed in her mind: proud, conceited, and convinced of his own superiority.

The evening is a triumph for everyone except Darcy. Bingley's sisters, Caroline and Mrs. Hurst, are elegant, fashionable, and quietly contemptuous of the country families, and Caroline in particular has set her cap at Darcy himself. She watches Elizabeth with jealous eyes, for she has noticed what Elizabeth has not: that Darcy, despite himself, keeps looking at the lively Bennet girl. When Elizabeth plays the pianoforte and sings, Darcy listens with an attention that surprises them both.

It is a brilliant misunderstanding, and entirely human. Darcy is not cruel; he is shy, awkward in company, and too honest to pretend admiration he does not feel. But Elizabeth has no way of knowing that, and she has every reason to believe the worst. She begins to collect evidence against him, and she finds a willing witness in the charming Mr. Wickham, a young officer who tells her a sad story of how Darcy cheated him out of his inheritance. Elizabeth believes every word, because it confirms what she already thinks.

Elizabeth's prejudice feeds on everything. When Darcy writes to his sister, she mocks his handwriting. When he is silent at dinner, she calls it pride. She spars with him in conversation, and he, to his own astonishment, enjoys it; no woman has ever dared to tease him before. There is a famous exchange in which she accuses him of having no compassion for the poor, and he answers her so gravely and so well that she is momentarily disarmed. But the armour goes straight back on. She has decided what he is, and she will not be moved.

Meanwhile, Jane and Bingley are falling genuinely in love, and Mrs. Bennet is in transports of delight. But Darcy, watching his friend, disapproves. He thinks Jane does not truly love Bingley, that the Bennet family is beneath them, and he quietly persuades Bingley to leave Netherfield and return to London. Jane is heartbroken. Elizabeth, learning of Darcy's interference, adds it to her catalogue of his crimes. By the time the Netherfield party scatters, Elizabeth Bennet's prejudice against Fitzwilliam Darcy is complete, confident, and almost entirely wrong.

Before the ball, there is the famous visit that shows Elizabeth at her best. Jane, caught in the rain on a visit to Netherfield, falls seriously ill and must stay there for days, and Elizabeth, refusing to wait for a carriage, walks the three miles through the mud to nurse her sister. She arrives with her petticoat six inches deep in mud, her hair disordered, her cheeks glowing, and the Bingley sisters sneer behind their fans. But Bingley is charmed, and Darcy, watching her tend Jane with such devoted affection, feels something shift in his chest. It is the first crack in his pride, and neither of them notices it happening.
chapters.title: The Netherfield Ball
The First Proposal
paragraphs: Months pass. Elizabeth visits her friend Charlotte, who has married the ridiculous Mr. Collins and settled at Hunsford parsonage, near the grand estate of Rosings, where Darcy's formidable aunt, Lady Catherine de Bourgh, reigns supreme. To Elizabeth's dismay, Darcy himself is visiting Rosings, and they meet constantly: at dinner, on walks, in the lanes. He seeks her out with a persistence that puzzles her, and his manner, once so cold, has become strangely intense.

Life at Hunsford is a comedy of condescension. Lady Catherine holds court at Rosings, dispensing advice on everything from pickles to pianofortes, and Mr. Collins bows and scrapes through every visit. Elizabeth endures it all with private amusement, but she is restless. Darcy calls at the parsonage with increasing frequency, restless too, though neither of them will admit why. They walk together, they argue about books and music, and every encounter leaves them both unsettled.

Colonel Fitzwilliam, Darcy's cousin, lets slip a piece of news that confirms all Elizabeth's suspicions: Darcy boasts of having separated Bingley from an unsuitable attachment, of saving his friend from an imprudent marriage. Elizabeth is furious. That evening, alone in the parsonage drawing room while rain beats against the windows, she hears a knock. Darcy enters, agitated, pale, and utterly unlike himself.

Fitzwilliam's revelation comes during a walk, dropped almost carelessly into conversation. He congratulates Darcy, he says, on saving Bingley from a most imprudent marriage, and he praises his cousin's talent for managing his friends' affairs. Elizabeth feels the blood rise to her face. So it was Darcy. It was Darcy who tore Jane from Bingley, who decided, in his arrogance, that the Bennets were not good enough. She walks home in a blaze of anger, and when Darcy appears that evening, she is ready for him, though nothing could have prepared her for what he is about to say.

What follows is one of the most famous scenes in all of literature. Darcy, who has been fighting his feelings for months, can fight no longer. He tells her that he has struggled in vain, that his feelings will not be repressed, that he must speak. "In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you." It is a declaration of overwhelming passion, and it is also, disastrously, an insult. For even as he confesses his love, he dwells on the inferiority of her family, the degradation of the match, the sacrifice he is making.

Elizabeth's answer is like a lightning strike. She refuses him, and she tells him exactly why: his arrogance, his cruelty to Wickham, his destruction of Jane's happiness. She throws his own pride back in his face with devastating precision. And then she delivers the line that has echoed through two centuries: "You are the last man in the world whom I could ever be prevailed on to marry." Darcy goes pale. He says nothing more. He bows and leaves, and Elizabeth, trembling, believes she has won a great victory. She has no idea that the battle has only just begun, and that it is being fought inside herself.

Elizabeth's rejection is a masterpiece of controlled fury. She accuses him of ruining Jane's happiness out of pure arrogance, of reducing Wickham to poverty out of resentment, of behaving everywhere with an unfeeling pride that no wealth can excuse. She tells him that his confession of love cannot compensate for the manner of it, that she has never desired his good opinion, and that he has bestowed it most unwillingly. Every word is a dagger, and every word is sincere. What she does not know, as she hurls these accusations, is that half of them are unjust, and that the man listening to them in white-faced silence already knows it, and loves her anyway.

chapters.title: Darcy's Letter
paragraphs: The next morning, as Elizabeth walks out alone, Darcy meets her on the lane and presses a letter into her hands. Then he is gone. She opens it with anger and curiosity, and what she reads destroys everything she thought she knew.

The letter is Darcy's defense, written with painful honesty. On the matter of Jane and Bingley, he admits his interference freely. He believed Jane indifferent, he says, and he believed the match imprudent; he acted to save his friend, and he would do it again. Elizabeth winces, but she cannot call it dishonourable. Then comes the story of Wickham, and here the ground opens beneath her feet. Wickham, Darcy reveals, is not the wronged innocent of Elizabeth's imagination but a liar, a gambler, and a predator. The living he claims Darcy stole was offered to him in money instead, which he squandered. And worse, far worse: Wickham once tried to elope with Darcy's young sister Georgiana, then fifteen, for her fortune alone.

Every fact checks out. Elizabeth remembers Wickham's evasions, his reluctance to meet Darcy, the pieces that never quite fit. She thinks of how eagerly she believed him, how she wanted Darcy to be a villain, and shame washes over her like a wave. She replays every conversation, every judgment, and sees herself with terrible clarity: blind, prejudiced, and proud of her own discernment most of all.

She walks for hours, the letter clutched in her hand, and by the time she returns, something fundamental has shifted. "Till this moment, I never knew myself," she thinks. It is the turning point of the novel, the moment the heroine's education truly begins. Her prejudice is not merely softened; it is shattered. And in its ruins, a new and reluctant feeling begins to grow: respect for the man she despised, and something warmer still, which she is not yet ready to name.

She reads the letter again the next day, and again, and each reading shifts the balance further. The facts about Wickham are damning and, she must admit, ring true: his sudden friendship, his eagerness to blacken Darcy's name, his debts, his pursuit of every heiress in the county. She remembers that Wickham never told his story to anyone who knew Darcy well, only to strangers like herself. And she remembers, with growing horror, how she repeated the slander to Jane, to Charlotte, to anyone who would listen. Her cleverness, her prized discernment, has made her the willing instrument of a scoundrel.

chapters.title: The Second Proposal
paragraphs: Elizabeth travels north with her aunt and uncle, the Gardiners, and by accident of itinerary they visit Pemberley, Darcy's magnificent estate. He is supposed to be away. He is not. They meet on the grounds, both mortified, and Elizabeth expects coldness. Instead she finds a Darcy transformed: gracious, attentive, kind to her relations, beloved by his servants. His housekeeper sings his praises. His sister Georgiana, shy and sweet, adores him. Elizabeth looks at the great house, the beautiful grounds, the portrait of Darcy in the gallery, and thinks, with a pang, of what she threw away.

Then disaster strikes. News comes that Lydia, the youngest Bennet sister, has eloped with none other than Wickham, and they are living in sin in London. The family's ruin seems certain: no respectable man will marry into such disgrace. Elizabeth is in despair, certain that Darcy, learning of it, will despise them all forever.

The portrait stops her cold. In the gallery at Pemberley hangs a painting of Darcy, and Elizabeth stands before it for a long time, studying the face she once hated. The artist has caught something she never saw in life: a softness around the eyes, a hint of vulnerability beneath the pride. Her uncle jokes that she might have been mistress of all this, and she laughs, but the laugh catches in her throat. For the first time she allows herself to imagine it, not as a fantasy of wealth, but as a life shared with the man she is only now beginning to understand.

But Darcy does something extraordinary. Secretly, at enormous expense, he finds the runaway couple, bribes Wickham with money and a commission, and forces the marriage that saves the Bennets' honour. He tells no one. Elizabeth learns of it only by accident, through Lydia's loose tongue, and she is overwhelmed. This is not the proud, selfish man of her prejudice. This is a man of profound generosity, who does good in secret and asks for nothing.

Lady Catherine's visit is the novel's great comic battle. The old tyrant sweeps into Longbourn unannounced, demands a private interview, and informs Elizabeth that a rumour of her engagement to Darcy has reached her. She requires Elizabeth to promise, on the spot, that she will never accept him. Elizabeth, who has faced down Darcy himself, is not about to yield to his aunt. She refuses, politely and immovably, and the more Lady Catherine rages, the calmer Elizabeth becomes. When the great lady finally storms out, Elizabeth is left shaken but triumphant, and entirely unaware that her defiance has just handed Darcy the hope he was waiting for.

The last obstacle is Darcy's terrible aunt. Lady Catherine storms down to Longbourn, having heard a rumour of an engagement, and demands that Elizabeth promise never to marry her nephew. Elizabeth refuses with magnificent spirit, and her defiance gives Darcy hope. He comes to her on an autumn morning as she walks out early, and this time there is no pride and no misunderstanding between them. "My affections and wishes are unchanged," he tells her, "but one word from you will silence me on this subject for ever."

Elizabeth's answer is everything he could wish. They talk for hours, explaining, confessing, laughing at their own blindness. Jane and Bingley, reunited, are engaged too. Mr. Bennet, told the news, can hardly believe that his favourite daughter has tamed the great Mr. Darcy, but he gives his blessing with tears in his eyes. The novel ends as all great comedies end: with marriages, with forgiveness, and with the quiet triumph of two people who have learned to see each other, and themselves, clearly at last.

Mr. Bennet's blessing, when it comes, is the novel's most touching scene. He calls Elizabeth into his study, certain she is marrying for money, and begs her not to do it. He cannot bear the thought of his favourite child trapped as he was. Elizabeth, laughing through tears, assures him that she loves and respects Darcy truly, and the old cynic is so moved that he gives his consent with a shaking hand. It is the first entirely honest conversation father and daughter have ever had, and it heals something in both of them. The proud man and the prejudiced girl have taught each other the hardest lesson of all: to see clearly, and to love what they see.

chapters.title: Pemberley
paragraphs: In the summer that followed the disaster at Hunsford, Elizabeth Bennet accepted an invitation that changed everything: a tour of the north of England with her aunt and uncle Gardiner, the sensible London relations she loved best in the world. The grand plan had been the Lakes, but time ran short, and they settled for Derbyshire instead, taking lodgings at Lambton, a small market town. One morning at breakfast, Mrs. Gardiner proposed a visit to Pemberley, the famous estate of Mr. Darcy, only ten miles away. Elizabeth felt the blood leave her face. She had refused that man, insulted him, and told him he was the last man in the world she could ever marry. The thought of walking through his house was unbearable, and she refused outright, until her aunt made inquiries of the chambermaid and learned that the Darcy family was away from home, the master himself expected only the day after their visit. What harm, Elizabeth told herself, in seeing a house whose owner would never know she had been there?

The approach to Pemberley astonished her. The park was vast and beautifully wooded, the ground rising and falling in natural grandeur, and a handsome stream wound through the valley, swelling into a lake where the banks were neither too formal nor too wild. Elizabeth, who had always loved the countryside, found herself admiring it in spite of herself. Every prospect seemed the work of nature rather than artifice, yet everything had been placed exactly right. She could not help thinking that the taste which had formed these grounds was not the taste of the proud, disagreeable man she had imagined. It was the taste of someone who understood beauty quietly, without showing off.

The house itself stood on rising ground above the water, a handsome stone building of beautiful proportions, neither too large for comfort nor too small for dignity. They were admitted by the housekeeper, Mrs. Reynolds, a respectable elderly woman with a kind face, who showed them through room after room. Everything was elegant without being ostentatious: fine pictures, handsome furniture, and everywhere the marks of a cultivated and generous mind. The Gardiners praised it all warmly. Elizabeth listened with a divided heart, for every beauty of the place was a quiet reproach. She had refused the master of all this, and at the time she had been glad of it.

Then Mrs. Reynolds began to speak of her master, and Elizabeth heard the portrait of a stranger. He was, the housekeeper declared, the best landlord and the best master who had ever lived, and nothing at all like the wild young men of the present day who thought of nobody but themselves. Some of his tenants spoke of him as a son might speak of a father. He had never had a cross word with her in all the years of her service. His sister adored him. His generosity was quiet and constant, and the poor of the parish knew his name as a friend. Elizabeth stood very still among the fine furniture, listening. This was not the proud, selfish man of her prejudice. This was a man loved by everyone who truly knew him, and she, who prided herself on her discernment, had known him least of all.

In the gallery they came at last to the family portraits, and there was Darcy himself, painted some years before, handsome and grave, with a softness in the expression that Elizabeth had never seen in life. She stood before it a long time while her uncle teased her, laughing that she was gazing a little too fondly at the master of Pemberley. She laughed too, but the laugh was hollow in her own ears. And then, unbidden, came the thought she could not drive away: this house, these grounds, this life might have been hers. She did not think it with greed or vanity. She thought it with a deep and aching regret, for she was beginning, at last, to understand whom she had refused.

As they drove away from Pemberley, Elizabeth's feelings were in complete turmoil. Contempt had been replaced by respect, and anger by gratitude for the painful honesty of his letter. Beneath it all, unacknowledged even to herself, something warmer was stirring, something she did not dare to name. She told herself that she was at least cured of her prejudice, and that this was enough. She did not know that Pemberley had one more surprise waiting for her, or that within a single day her whole world would be turned upside down.

Mrs. Gardiner had a particular reason for wishing to see Pemberley. She had spent her girlhood in Lambton itself, and she remembered the Darcy family of those days, though she had left the neighborhood before the present master grew to manhood. She spoke of old Mr. Darcy with respect, and of young Fitzwilliam as a fine, proud boy, and Elizabeth listened with a strange mixture of dread and curiosity. To hear of Darcy as a child, from someone who had known his people before wealth and consequence had set their stamp on him, made him seem suddenly human and reachable, almost familiar. Elizabeth found herself asking questions she had not meant to ask, and her aunt answered them with an arch smile that Elizabeth chose not to notice.

Elizabeth could not resist asking, as casually as she could manage, about Mr. Wickham, and Mrs. Reynolds's kind face changed at once. Wickham had been the late steward's son, she said, raised almost as a companion to young Mr. Darcy, and her old master had been very fond of the boy. But he had turned out wild, extravagant, and ungrateful, a sore trial to everyone who had hoped better of him. Elizabeth listened with her heart beating fast, for here was independent confirmation of everything Darcy had written in his letter. The housekeeper had no reason to lie and no quarrel to pursue. Wickham was exactly what Darcy had said he was, and Elizabeth felt the last of her old doubts dissolve into shame.

Mrs. Reynolds showed them a miniature of Miss Darcy as well, a sweet-faced girl of sixteen, and spoke of her young mistress with almost maternal pride. She was shy, the housekeeper said, but everything that was good and gentle, and devoted to her brother beyond anything. Elizabeth studied the little portrait and thought of the letter's dreadful revelation: that Wickham had once tried to lure this innocent girl into an elopement for her fortune. The thought made her shudder. How eagerly she herself had believed Wickham's lies, how readily she had repeated them. Her cleverness, her prized discernment, had made her the willing instrument of a scoundrel, and she felt the shame of it like a physical weight.

On the drive back to Lambton, the Gardiners talked of nothing but Pemberley and its master. Mr. Gardiner declared he had never seen a place so beautifully kept, and Mrs. Gardiner confessed she was charmed by everything she had heard of Mr. Darcy. If half of what Mrs. Reynolds had said was true, he was one of the most estimable men in England. Elizabeth agreed quietly and said very little more, but her thoughts were in a whirl. The man the whole neighborhood called proud and disagreeable was beloved by his servants, generous to his tenants, and adored by his sister. Either the world was wrong about him, or she had been. She was beginning to suspect, with a sinking heart, that it was she.

chapters.title: The Gentleman from the Lake
paragraphs: They had barely begun their walk through the Pemberley grounds when Elizabeth's uncle stopped and stared. A gentleman on horseback was coming down the path toward them, and as he drew nearer, Elizabeth's heart nearly stopped. It was Darcy himself, arrived a day earlier than expected, and he looked nothing like the master of a great estate. He was on foot now, having left his horse, and he was coming up from the lake below, his clothes damp and disordered, his hair wet, mud on his boots. He had clearly been swimming or fishing and had not expected to meet anyone. For a moment they simply stared at each other, both equally mortified, both equally unable to speak.

Then, to Elizabeth's utter astonishment, Darcy recovered himself and behaved with a civility she had never seen in him. There was no coldness, no pride, no trace of the haughty man of the Meryton assembly. He greeted her with genuine warmth, asked after her family with real interest, and when she introduced the Gardiners, he received them as honored guests rather than as strangers of no consequence. He begged their permission to introduce his sister to them the next day, and spoke of Elizabeth to them with such evident regard that her aunt and uncle exchanged glances of surprise. Elizabeth could hardly believe her senses. This was a transformation so complete that she wondered if she had ever known him at all.

The next day the Gardiners were presented to Miss Darcy, and Elizabeth saw at once why her brother loved her so. Georgiana was sixteen, shy almost to the point of silence, pretty, gentle, and sweet, and she looked at Elizabeth with an admiration that was plainly her brother's doing. She had heard so much of Miss Elizabeth Bennet that she seemed to regard her as something wonderful. Caroline Bingley was there too, elegant and watchful, and Elizabeth saw the jealousy in her eyes. When Caroline tried to wound her with a pointed remark about Wickham and the militia, Darcy answered so firmly in Elizabeth's defense that Caroline fell silent. Elizabeth felt a rush of something she had never felt before: the sensation of being protected by the very man she had once despised.

The very morning the dreadful letters arrived, Elizabeth had written home to Jane in the highest spirits. Her letter was full of Pemberley: the beauty of the grounds, the elegance of the house, Mrs. Reynolds's extraordinary praise of her master, and, above all, the astonishing transformation in Darcy himself. She described his civility to the Gardiners, his tenderness toward Georgiana, and Georgiana's shy admiration for her new acquaintance. She sealed the letter with a light heart and sent it off by the morning post, little knowing that before the day was out she would be writing another letter entirely, and that Jane would read the two together with a breaking heart.

That evening at the inn in Lambton, two letters arrived from Jane, and Elizabeth's new happiness collapsed in an instant. The first letter, written days earlier, spoke of Lydia's growing wildness at Brighton. The second contained the catastrophe: Lydia had eloped with Wickham. They had run away together, and though pursuit had been made, they had vanished, believed to be hiding in London, unmarried. Jane wrote in anguish of their mother's hysterics, their father's grim silence, and the ruin that would fall on them all. For a girl who ran away with a man outside marriage was ruined, and her sisters were ruined with her. No respectable man would marry into such a family. Elizabeth read the letters with shaking hands, her face white. She thought of Jane, of her father, of everything they would suffer, and she thought, with a bitterness that cut like a knife, that she had known Wickham's true character for months and had told no one, out of pride, out of a foolish wish to spare Darcy's name.

She had barely finished reading when Darcy himself was announced. He had come, all civility, to ask whether she would allow his sister to call on her the next morning. Elizabeth, her eyes red and her composure shattered, could not hide her distress. He asked what was wrong, and in her agitation she told him, blurting out the whole dreadful story before she could stop herself: Lydia's elopement, Wickham's villainy, the disgrace that would destroy them all. Darcy listened in grave silence, his face growing paler with every word. When she finished, he said very little. He expressed his concern, promised nothing, and took his leave almost at once. Elizabeth watched him go with a sinking heart. He had seen, at last, the full measure of her family's disgrace, and she was certain she had lost him forever. Whatever tenderness had been growing between them, Lydia's folly had killed it in a single afternoon.

The following evening the Gardiners dined at Pemberley, and Elizabeth had the chance to observe the brother and sister together. Georgiana, though painfully shy with strangers, bloomed in her brother's presence, and Darcy watched over her with a tenderness that Elizabeth found deeply moving. After dinner Darcy asked Elizabeth to play the pianoforte, and she complied, conscious of Georgiana's admiring eyes and Caroline Bingley's cold stare. When Caroline made a pointed remark about the militia's departure from Meryton, clearly meant to remind everyone of Wickham, Elizabeth answered with perfect composure, and she saw Darcy look at her with something very like admiration. She went to bed that night happier than she had been in months.

She did not sleep. She lay awake rereading Jane's letters until the words blurred, and with every reading her self-reproach grew sharper. She remembered Wickham's sudden attentions to Miss King, an heiress of ten thousand pounds, remembered his debts and his evasions, remembered how he had vanished whenever Darcy appeared. She had known, or half-known, all of it, and she had said nothing, telling herself it was delicacy toward Darcy that kept her silent. It was not delicacy. It was pride, the same pride that had made her believe Wickham's lies in the first place, and now her whole family would pay for it.

When Elizabeth told her aunt and uncle what had happened, Mr. Gardiner resolved to go to London at once to join Mr. Bennet in the search, and Mrs. Gardiner wept for poor Jane. They would leave Derbyshire immediately. Elizabeth packed her things with numb hands, thinking only of Darcy. He had come to the inn full of courtesy and kindness, and she had repaid him with the news of her family's ruin. She would never see him again, she was certain. Whatever had been growing between them at Pemberley was over, killed by Lydia's folly before it had ever truly begun.

chapters.title: The Elopement
paragraphs: Elizabeth and the Gardiners hurried back to Longbourn as fast as horses could carry them, and found the house in a state of chaos. Mrs. Bennet had taken to her room, where she lay on her sofa in a darkened chamber, alternating between floods of tears and fits of hysterical railing. She declared she would never see Lydia again, and in the next breath wept that her poor child would be ruined and starving in the streets of London. She reproached her husband, her daughters, the servants, and Providence itself, all in the same breathless torrent. Her nerves, she announced, were shattered beyond repair, and she would never survive the disgrace.

Mr. Bennet, for once in his life, was not amused by anything. The easy sarcasm had gone out of him, replaced by a grim and silent self-reproach. He blamed himself, and justly, for years of indulgent neglect. He had laughed at Lydia's wildness instead of restraining it, had let her go to Brighton against every warning, and now his youngest daughter was lost. Without a word of comfort to anyone, he set off for London to search for the fugitives himself, accompanied by Mr. Gardiner, who had come up from town to help. Day after day they searched, advertised, questioned, and bribed, and day after day they found nothing. Wickham had covered his tracks well, and London was very large.

At Longbourn, Jane and Elizabeth clung to each other in their despair. Jane, gentle as ever, tried to hope that Wickham might still mean to marry Lydia, that there might be some misunderstanding, some explanation that would save them. Elizabeth could not share the hope. She knew Wickham now for what he was: a gambler, a liar, a man without honor or principle, who had tried to ruin Darcy's young sister for her fortune and would not hesitate to ruin Lydia for his pleasure. And she knew, with a guilt that gnawed at her day and night, that she had possessed this knowledge for months and had kept it to herself. If she had exposed Wickham when she first learned the truth, Lydia might never have trusted him. She confessed it all to Jane, weeping, and Jane comforted her as best she could, though Elizabeth could not be comforted.

Mary, meanwhile, moralized. She produced sententious observations about the wages of imprudence and the importance of female virtue, which comforted nobody. Kitty wept and was scolded for weeping, and then wept again. The whole neighborhood buzzed with the scandal, and every visitor brought a fresh supply of pity thinly disguised as curiosity. Mrs. Bennet, between her fits, tormented herself with visions of the future: Jane and Elizabeth would never marry now, no man of sense would connect himself to such a family, and they would all end as poor spinsters living on charity. Even Elizabeth, usually so resilient, began to fear her mother was right. The disgrace of one sister, in that unforgiving world, was the disgrace of all.

Then, after two weeks of silence, a letter came from Mr. Gardiner in London, and the news was so unexpected that nobody dared believe it at first. Lydia was found. Wickham had agreed to marry her. The wedding would take place within days, quietly, in London, and the couple would then join Wickham's new regiment in the north. Mrs. Bennet's despair turned in an instant to rapturous triumph. Her daughter married! A wedding! She forgot every tear she had shed, forgave Lydia everything, and threw herself into ecstasies over wedding clothes and carriages, as if the past fortnight had never happened. Mr. Bennet returned home exhausted and strangely subdued, and Elizabeth, watching him, felt that something in her father had been broken for good.

The details, when they emerged, were sordid and complete. Lydia had left Brighton with Wickham in a hired chaise, leaving behind a letter for her friend Mrs. Forster announcing gaily that she was going to Gretna Green to be married. It was a lie, or at best a fantasy. No marriage followed. The pair were traced as far as London and then lost entirely. Colonel Forster wrote to Mr. Bennet with everything he knew, and it was damning: Wickham was heavily in debt, had left gambling debts all over Brighton, and had no intention, in the colonel's opinion, of marrying any girl without a fortune. Lydia, giddy and infatuated, had thrown herself away on a man who valued her at nothing.

When Mr. Bennet returned from London empty-handed, he was a changed man. The sarcasm was gone, the easy laughter was gone, and in their place was a heavy, bitter gravity that frightened his daughters more than any anger could have. He blamed himself openly now and would not be comforted. He had been an indolent father, he said, and his children had paid the price. Elizabeth, seeing him so broken, felt her heart ache for him even as she shared his guilt. They had all failed Lydia in their different ways: he through neglect, her mother through indulgence, and Elizabeth through silence.

The neighborhood, of course, talked of nothing else. Mrs. Philips brought every scrap of gossip she could gather, Sir William Lucas looked solemn, and even Charlotte, kind and sensible, could offer Jane nothing but sympathy. Elizabeth bore it all with outward composure and inward torment. She thought of her parents' marriage, the root of every evil: a clever man who had married a fool and punished her for it with twenty years of mockery, leaving five daughters to raise themselves. Lydia was the harvest of that marriage, and they were all reaping it now.

In her darkest moments Elizabeth imagined the future entire: the entail taking Longbourn to Mr. Collins at her father's death, her mother turned out, her sisters portionless, Jane's sweetness wasted, her own hopes gone. It was a vision of genteel ruin, and it haunted her sleep. Only Jane's steadfastness kept her from despair altogether. Jane never reproached anyone, never lost her gentleness, and prayed daily for Lydia's safety with a faith Elizabeth could not share. Watching her sister, Elizabeth understood at last what true goodness looked like. It was not cleverness. It was not wit. It was Jane, enduring everything and blaming no one.

chapters.title: A Secret Benefactor
paragraphs: Elizabeth could not rejoice as freely as the rest of the family, for one question troubled her mind and would not let her rest. Wickham was penniless, deep in debt, with creditors in every town where the militia had been quartered. Such a man did not marry a portionless girl out of love, and he certainly did not do it cheaply. Yet Mr. Gardiner's letter spoke of the settlement as a modest affair: Wickham's debts paid, a commission purchased for him in a regular regiment, and a small allowance settled on Lydia. It was far too little to tempt a scoundrel like Wickham into marriage. Someone, Elizabeth suspected, had paid a great deal more than Mr. Gardiner admitted, and she could not imagine who would do such a thing, or why.

The answer came, as answers so often do in this family, through Lydia's own loose tongue. The newly married Mrs. Wickham came to Longbourn to show off her wedding ring and her consequence, chattering with her usual thoughtlessness, and in the middle of her boasting she let slip a name that froze Elizabeth's blood. Mr. Darcy had been at the wedding. Mr. Darcy, of all people, had been present when Lydia married Wickham, had arranged everything, had even, Lydia giggled, been cross and disagreeable about it. Elizabeth pressed her for more, but Lydia, reminded by her husband's warning looks that she was not supposed to tell, would say nothing further. It was enough. Elizabeth's heart pounded as the truth assembled itself in her mind, piece by piece, each piece more astonishing than the last.

She wrote at once to her aunt Gardiner, begging for the whole truth, and Mrs. Gardiner's reply confirmed everything. It was Darcy who had found the fugitives in London, Darcy who had traced Wickham through his debts and his haunts, Darcy who had negotiated with the scoundrel, paid his gambling debts, purchased his commission, and bribed him with a handsome sum into marrying Lydia. He had done it all in secret, insisting that Mr. Gardiner take the public credit, and he had forbidden anyone to tell Elizabeth. Mrs. Gardiner wrote that she had never witnessed such generosity, such delicacy, such complete disregard for his own interest. Reading the letter, Elizabeth felt as though the ground were shifting beneath her feet. This, she thought with wonder, was a stroke of civility she had never expected, from the man she had once called the proudest creature in the world.

She sat for a long time with the letter in her hands, and everything she had ever thought about Darcy rearranged itself. He had done this knowing that Lydia's disgrace had touched his own prospects, knowing that Elizabeth's family was now more disreputable than ever, knowing that he could expect nothing in return. He had done it, she understood at last, simply because it was right, and because he loved her, though he believed she could never be his. There was no pride in this act, no vanity, no calculation. It was pure, secret goodness, the kind that asks for no witness and no reward. And Elizabeth, who had prided herself on seeing through everyone, realized that she had never truly seen this man until now.

From that hour, Elizabeth's feelings underwent their final transformation. Respect had become admiration, admiration had become gratitude, and gratitude was rapidly becoming something far more tender. She thought of his letter, of Pemberley, of his kindness to the Gardiners, of his defense of her against Caroline Bingley, and now of this last and greatest proof of his character. She loved him. She admitted it to herself at last, plainly and without reservation. And with the admission came a sharp and aching regret, for she believed she had lost him. He had seen her family's deepest shame. He had paid a fortune to repair it. And he had walked away without a word, asking nothing. What man, having done so much, would ever return to ask for more?

Lydia herself arrived at Longbourn a few days later, a married woman of sixteen, and her behavior was a fresh mortification. She showed off her wedding ring to everyone, demanded to be called Mrs. Wickham, took precedence over her unmarried sisters with absurd pomposity, and spoke of her husband with a giggling admiration that made Elizabeth's skin crawl. She had not a blush of shame for what she had done, not a thought for what her family had suffered. Elizabeth looked at her youngest sister and felt pity rather than anger. Lydia was not wicked. She was simply empty, a child who had never been taught to think, and Wickham had filled the emptiness with flattery.

Mrs. Gardiner's letter, when it came, laid the whole affair bare with a frankness that left Elizabeth breathless. Darcy had paid Wickham's debts, which amounted to more than a thousand pounds. He had purchased Wickham's commission in a northern regiment. He had settled a further sum on the couple and secured a small allowance for Lydia. The total was staggering, a fortune spent on a scoundrel, and Darcy had done it all quietly, through Mr. Gardiner, insisting that his name never be mentioned. He had even attended the wedding himself, to make certain Wickham went through with it. Elizabeth read the figures twice, hardly able to comprehend such generosity toward a man Darcy had every reason to despise.

In the days that followed, Elizabeth examined her own heart with the same ruthless honesty she had once turned on Darcy. Was this love, or only gratitude? She thought of Pemberley, of the grounds she had admired, of the housekeeper's praise, of Georgiana's shy admiration, of Darcy's transformed manners, of his defense of her against Caroline Bingley. She thought of his letter, painful and honest, and of the man who had written it. And she knew, at last, that it was love, real and complete, founded not on fancy or vanity but on the deepest respect and admiration she had ever felt. She loved him. And she believed, with a grief that never quite left her, that she had lost him forever.

chapters.title: Lady Catherine at Dawn
paragraphs: The morning had begun like any other at Longbourn. Elizabeth was in the drawing room with Jane when the servant announced, with visible awe, that Lady Catherine de Bourgh was in the carriage outside and desired to see Miss Elizabeth Bennet. Mrs. Bennet fluttered into a panic of raptures and confusion, offering tea and refreshments, which her ladyship declined with freezing politeness. Lady Catherine swept past them all without sitting down, her eyes fixed on Elizabeth, and demanded a private interview at once. There was something in her manner, rigid and barely controlled, that told Elizabeth this was no social call.

Elizabeth had been home only a few weeks when, very early one morning, the servants announced a visitor, and Lady Catherine de Bourgh swept into the Longbourn drawing room like a thunderstorm. She had come, she announced without preamble, all the way from Rosings on urgent business, and she required a private interview with Miss Elizabeth Bennet immediately. Elizabeth, bewildered but composed, led her out to the garden walk, where they could speak undisturbed. What followed was the most extraordinary confrontation of Elizabeth's life.

Lady Catherine came directly to the point. A rumor had reached her, she said, of the most alarming and disgraceful kind: that her nephew, Mr. Darcy, was to be engaged to Elizabeth Bennet. She demanded to know whether the rumor was true, and when Elizabeth declined to answer a question so impertinently put, the great lady's fury knew no bounds. She lectured Elizabeth on the vast distance between their stations, on the insult to Darcy's family, on the sacred engagement she had always intended between Darcy and her own daughter. And then she made her demand: Elizabeth must promise, here and now, never to enter into such an engagement, never to accept her nephew's hand.

Elizabeth refused. She refused politely, she refused firmly, and she refused absolutely. She was a gentleman's daughter, she said, and Mr. Darcy was a gentleman, and she would make no promise to surrender her own judgment to anyone's dictates. The more Lady Catherine raged, the calmer Elizabeth became. The great lady called her ungrateful, scheming, and artful; she declared that the shades of Pemberley itself would be polluted by such a union, and demanded to know whether Elizabeth had no regard for Darcy's honor, his family, his name. Elizabeth answered that she had every regard for them, and that her own conduct would be guided by her own conscience, not by Lady Catherine's commands.

At last Lady Catherine, trembling with rage, delivered her final ultimatum, and Elizabeth delivered her final answer. She would make no promise of the kind demanded. She was resolved, she said, to act in that manner which would constitute her own happiness, without reference to anyone but herself, and if her choice should displease Lady Catherine, the great lady must learn to bear it. It was a declaration of independence as bold as anything Elizabeth had ever uttered, bolder even than her rejection of Darcy himself, for this time she was defending not her pride but her freedom. Lady Catherine stared at her in disbelief, pronounced her the most obstinate and ungrateful girl in England, and stormed back to her carriage without another word.

When the carriage had rattled away, Elizabeth stood alone on the gravel walk, shaken but triumphant. She had faced down the most formidable woman of her acquaintance and had not yielded an inch. But as her heartbeat slowed, a new thought struck her, and it struck her with force. How had Lady Catherine heard this rumor? Someone must have spoken of Darcy and Elizabeth as a possible match, someone close enough to Darcy to know his feelings. And if Darcy had not given up hope, if he still cared, then perhaps, just perhaps, her own hope was not as dead as she had believed. She walked back to the house in a tumult of feeling, hardly daring to put her new thought into words, even to herself.

Long after the carriage had gone, Elizabeth sat alone trying to make sense of what had happened. Lady Catherine's fury had been real, which meant her fear was real, which meant the rumor had substance. Someone had seen something, heard something, that made even that proud old woman believe Darcy meant to marry Elizabeth Bennet. Elizabeth thought of Darcy's grave face at the inn in Lambton, of the fortune he had spent on Lydia without asking for thanks. A man did not do such things for a woman he had ceased to love. Hope, which she had buried so carefully, began to stir again, timid and unwilling, like a seed in winter ground.

She told Jane everything that evening, and Jane listened with wide eyes, astonished first by Lady Catherine's insolence and then by Elizabeth's defiance. But what amazed Jane most was the confession that followed: that Elizabeth loved Darcy, had loved him for months, and had believed him lost. Jane, who had always seen Darcy as proud and cold, could hardly comprehend it, but she took Elizabeth's hands and said, with all her gentle earnestness, that if Mr. Darcy truly loved her sister, he must be a better man than anyone had supposed, and she hoped with all her heart that he would come. Elizabeth smiled through tears she had not known were falling, and for the first time in weeks she allowed herself to hope.

From that day Elizabeth watched every visitor, listened for every piece of news, and started at every carriage on the road. She told herself she was foolish, that hope was a luxury she could not afford. But hope, once awakened, refused to sleep again.

chapters.title: Two Weddings
paragraphs: Autumn came, and with it news that set Longbourn buzzing: Mr. Bingley was returning to Netherfield, and Mr. Darcy was coming with him. Mrs. Bennet was thrown into transports. Jane turned pale and then pink and said very little. Within days Bingley was calling at Longbourn, and it was plain to everyone that his feelings for Jane were exactly what they had always been. This time there were no interferences and no misunderstandings. He proposed, Jane accepted him with all the warmth of her gentle heart, and the house erupted in joy. Mrs. Bennet's ecstasies knew no bounds: her beautiful Jane engaged to a man of fortune, and at last, at last, one daughter settled.

Elizabeth watched her sister's happiness with a full heart and a secret ache, for she had by now confessed everything to Jane: her changed feelings, her love for Darcy, her conviction that she had lost him forever. Jane, who had always thought Darcy proud and disagreeable, listened in amazement, and then, with her usual sweetness, told Elizabeth that she had never been so surprised in her life, and that she hoped with all her heart that Elizabeth might be mistaken about having lost him. Elizabeth smiled sadly and said she did not dare to hope.

She was wrong to despair. One fine autumn morning, Elizabeth walked out early, as was her habit, and on turning a corner of the lane she came face to face with Darcy himself. He had come, he told her, with a purpose he could no longer delay. His affections and wishes, he said, were unchanged from what he had declared at Hunsford, but one word from her would silence him on the subject forever. Elizabeth, her heart pounding, gave him the word he longed to hear. She told him that her feelings had undergone a complete change, that she loved and respected him, and she asked his forgiveness for the injustice she had done him. They walked together for hours, explaining everything, confessing everything, laughing at their own blindness. He told her, at last, how her defiance of Lady Catherine had reached him through his aunt's furious account, and how it had given him the hope he had scarcely dared to feel. Elizabeth laughed through her tears at the thought that she owed her happiness to Lady Catherine herself.

There remained one trial: her father. Mr. Bennet sent for Elizabeth and received her in his study with a grave face. He had heard the news, he said, and he could not believe it. Darcy was a proud, disagreeable man, and Elizabeth, his cleverest child, could not possibly love him. He begged her, with an earnestness she had never seen in him, not to marry for money, not to sacrifice herself as he had sacrificed himself in his own unhappy marriage. Elizabeth, laughing and crying together, assured him that she loved Darcy truly, respected him deeply, and was marrying for love alone. Mr. Bennet studied her face for a long moment, and then, to his own astonishment, he believed her. He gave his consent with tears in his eyes, and father and daughter shared the first entirely honest conversation of their lives.

The weddings, when they came, were the triumph of Mrs. Bennet's existence. Jane married Bingley and Elizabeth married Darcy on fine winter days, and Mrs. Bennet talked of nothing else for months: the carriages, the clothes, the settlements, the wonderful good fortune of her daughters. She boasted to all of Netherfield and half of Derbyshire, and was perfectly, completely happy. Kitty, taken often to stay with her married sisters, lost much of her silliness in better company and became a sensible young woman. Mary, left at home, continued her moralizing over her books and her pianoforte, undisturbed and undisturbing. Even Lady Catherine, after a suitable interval of offended dignity, was brought to accept the inevitable, and condescended at last to visit Pemberley and admire the improvements, as though the whole match had been her own idea all along.

Darcy's formal visit to Longbourn to ask Mr. Bennet's consent was an ordeal for everyone, though Elizabeth laughed about it afterward. Mr. Bennet, still half-convinced his daughter was bewitched or mercenary, received his future son-in-law with a bewildered gravity that bordered on the comic, and Darcy, for all his wealth and consequence, was as nervous as a schoolboy. But the interview ended well, and Mr. Bennet emerged from his study shaking his head in wonder, telling his wife that if any man could deserve Elizabeth, it was this one, and that he had never been so surprised in his life, which, from Mr. Bennet, was high praise indeed.

The engagement was announced, and the reactions were everything Elizabeth had expected and more. Caroline Bingley wrote a letter of congratulation so stiff with resentment that Elizabeth could only laugh. Georgiana wrote with girlish delight, already calling Elizabeth her sister. The Gardiners were overjoyed, and Mrs. Gardiner confessed she had suspected something ever since Pemberley. Even Mr. Collins wrote, with his usual pomposity, to warn Elizabeth of Lady Catherine's displeasure, which made her laugh until she cried.

Mrs. Bennet's behavior during the wedding preparations was a spectacle the neighborhood would remember for years. She boasted to Lady Lucas until that lady could barely contain herself, ordered clothes enough for a duchess, and talked of Pemberley and its ten thousand a year until Elizabeth begged her to stop. But Elizabeth bore it all with unusual patience, for she understood at last that her mother's folly came from love, however misguided, and that beneath the vulgarity was a woman who had lived in fear for her daughters for twenty years and could finally rest.

The wedding day itself was all brightness. Elizabeth walked to the altar with a heart so full she could barely speak her vows, and Darcy, grave and radiant together, held her hand as though he would never let it go. Jane, lovely in her own happiness, wept quietly through the service. Afterward there was a breakfast at Longbourn at which Mrs. Bennet outdid herself, and then the carriages, and the farewells, and the long road north to Pemberley. Elizabeth looked back once at the house where she had grown up, and then forward, toward the life waiting for her, and she did not look back again.

And Elizabeth and Darcy? They settled at Pemberley in a happiness so complete that it surprised even themselves. The Gardiners, to whom Elizabeth owed so much, remained their dearest friends and most welcome guests. Darcy learned playfulness from his wife, and Elizabeth learned judgment from her husband, and each taught the other the lesson the novel had been teaching all along: that first impressions deceive, that pride blinds, and that true understanding, once earned through humility and honesty, is the surest foundation for love. They had begun as the proudest man and the most prejudiced woman in England. They ended as two people who saw each other, and themselves, clearly at last, and loved what they saw.
